newsitem.title: USA: Committee hears of Trie's cash for Clinton defense.
newsitem.headline: Committee hears of Trie's cash for Clinton defense.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent

Former Little Rock restaurant owner Yah Lin "Charlie" Trie appeared in the office of President Bill Clinton's personal legal defence fund in March 1996 and dumped $460,000 on the table, a Senate committee heard on Wednesday.

Michael Cardozo, executive director of the Presidential Legal Expense Trust, told the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee how Trie tried to donate three huge sums of money, which he said came from the Asian American community, and how all the contributions were eventually rejected.
The committee is investigating how foreign money, mostly from Asian business interests, illegally flowed into 1996 political campaigns and whether U.S. security was damaged or favours bought.
Questioned by majority counsel Mark Tipps, Cardozo said he was suspicious about the source of the money from the first.
"Mr. Trie advised me he was a friend of the president's from Little Rock, Arkansas and that he was concerned about the president's mounting legal bills," Cardozo said.

Clinton and his wife have run up millions of dollars in legal fees relating to their involvement in the Whitewater land affair and a sexual harrassment suit filed against Clinton by former Arkansas state employee Paula Corbin Jones.
"Mr. Trie then stated that he had collected contributions for the Trust in the form of checks and money orders totalling about $460,000 from the Asian-American community," Cardozo said.

Republicans asked Cardozo why his suspicions about Trie were not picked up by White House officials or passed on to the Democratic Party. He said his main interest was not Trie, but who stood behind him and what was the source of the money.

At roughly the same time as he tried to give money to the Trust, Trie also gave $220,000 in illegal laundered funds, from an Asian businessman who has connections to China, to the Democratic National Committee which accepted the money and only returned it this year.

Utah Sen. Robert Bennett said: "You smelled a rat when you met Charlie Trie ... The folks at the White House and the DNC allowed him to enter the White House 23 times and didn't seem to have the sense and antennae that you did."

Republicans also expressed suspicion that the Trust altered its bi-annual report in June 1996 in order to keep Trie's abortive contributions secret until after the November 1996 presidential election.
But Ohio Democrat Sen. John Glenn said: "I think your performance was admirable and so was the performance of the White House."

Trie met Clinton when he owned a Little Rock Chinese restaurant. When Clinton was elected president in 1992, Trie moved to Washington, hoping to turn his acquaintance with Clinton into business opportunities.
Trie took refuge in China some time late last year and has refused to cooperate with the investigation.

Cardozo said he briefed first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton in April, 1996 about Trie's contributions but she barely remembered him. Senior White House official Harold Ickes, who was also at that meeting, was busy taking notes and did not say anything.

The Trust hired a firm of investigators to look into the source of the money and found that most of the contributions were raised at meetings of the Ching Hai Buddhist sect which, Cardozo said, had been described by some as a cult.
Later in April, Trie tried to give an additional $179,000 which he brought to Cardozo's office in a bag.
"It was a large shopping bag, he was heavily laden, and I thought, 'Oh my God, he's got a million dollars in there'," Cardozo testified.
Also in the bag were inflatable cola bottles and cushions which Trie wanted Cardozo to help him market. Cardozo said he declined the opportunity.
Later, Trie tried to give yet another $150,000.
Cardozo insisted that White House officials put no pressure on the Trust either to accept or reject the money and that both Clintons supported his decision to return it.
